goals: Identify supply chain risks by function and by type, including hidden dependencies.
Score risks by probability and impact, and draw a heat map.
Choose a strategy for each risk: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept.
Write contingency plans with triggers, owners and a review rhythm.
Explain resilience: visibility, agility and options, using real disruptions.
Include cyber risk and documentation risk in the risk register.

handout.intro: Every supply chain will be disrupted. Risk management does not stop disruptions; it makes sure that when they come, you already know what to do. This session builds a risk management plan step by step, using real events.

blocks.p: Any event that can stop the flow of products, information or money. Risks move along the chain: a supplier delay becomes a stock problem, then a warehouse problem, then a late delivery, then a customer complaint.

head: Type
Examples
rows: Operational
Machine breakdown, picking errors, IT failure, staff shortage
Financial
Supplier bankruptcy, currency changes, sudden cost increases
Compliance
Wrong customs documents, new regulations
External
Storms, pandemics, port strikes, conflicts, blocked shipping routes
Cyber
Ransomware or malware that stops systems

blocks.p: Go through each function (procurement, inventory, warehouse, transport, trade) and each risk type. Ask people at every level: drivers, buyers and supervisors know risks that never reach reports.

callout.title: Hidden dependencies
callout.text: You have two suppliers for a part, so you feel safe. But both buy their raw material from the **same** factory. You have not removed the single point of failure; you have only moved it one step upstream. Ask: **what is connected to what?**

blocks.p: Record each risk in a **risk register**: number, description, function, type, warning signs, owner.
Score each risk from 1 to 5 for **probability** (how likely) and **impact** (how bad). **Risk score = probability × impact** (1–25).

head: Score
Level
Action
rows: Critical
Act now. Named owner and trigger.
High
Reduce soon: backup supplier, buffer stock, another route.
Medium
Reduce or prepare a contingency plan.
Low
Accept and monitor.

blocks.p: Plot the risks on a 5 × 5 **heat map** to see which ones to act on first. Try the **Risk score and heat map** tool.

head: Strategy
Meaning
Example
rows: Avoid
Change the plan so the risk is gone
Stop buying from a region at war
Reduce
Lower the probability or the impact
Second supplier, safety stock, preventive maintenance
Transfer
Pass the cost to someone else
Cargo insurance, contract clauses
Accept
Live with it and watch it
A small, rare risk that costs more to fix than to accept

blocks.p: A **trigger** is a signal decided in advance that starts an action automatically. Example: “If a hurricane warning is issued within 200 km of our supplier’s plant, place the standby order with our backup supplier the same day.” A trigger turns a hard decision under pressure into a **decision already made**.

list: Each priority risk: strategy, owner, trigger, first actions, who to tell.
Test the plan (a desk exercise) before you need it.
Review the register **monthly** for operational risks and **quarterly** for strategic risks, and after every disruption.

head: Event
What happened
Lesson
rows: Qatar, June 2017
Land border and usual transhipment routes closed overnight; new direct sea routes via Oman, India and Turkey in days
Have more than one route ready before you need it
Maersk cyber attack, June 2017
The NotPetya malware shut down the shipping line’s IT systems for days
Back up data, plan to work without systems, practise recovery
Factories closed, demand jumped for some products and collapsed for others, panic buying
Demand shocks need visibility and flexible capacity
Ever Given, March 2021
One ship blocked the Suez Canal for about six days; hundreds of ships waited
Single routes are single points of failure
Red Sea, from late 2023
Attacks on ships sent most Asia–Europe container traffic around Africa, adding time and cost
Plan longer lead times and compare suppliers by route risk

blocks.p: Read the full Ever Given, Red Sea and Qatar 2017 cases in **Tools → Case studies**.

list: **Visibility** – know where your stock, shipments, suppliers and orders are today, not at the end of the month.
**Agility** – the ability to change quickly: other suppliers, routes, modes and markets.
**Options cost money** – a backup supplier or extra stock you may not use is the price of resilience. The most efficient chain is often not the most resilient.

blocks.p: Two useful questions for each critical supplier or site: **How long would it take to recover if it stopped?** and **How long can we keep serving customers without it?** If recovery takes longer than you can survive, act now.
Stock risk is not only running out: it is also **too much** stock, expiry, theft and wrong records. Do not panic-buy in a crisis: it creates overstock later (the bullwhip effect).

A wrong document can stop a container as surely as a storm. Check requirements before each shipment, keep templates up to date, and train more than one person on customs paperwork, so knowledge does not leave with one employee.

terms.meaning: Any event that could stop the flow of products, information or money.
terms.example: A port strike at the destination.

terms.meaning: One part whose failure stops the whole chain.
terms.example: One supplier, one port or one route.

terms.meaning: Action that lowers the probability or impact of a risk.
Passing the cost of a risk to another party.
A plan ready for when a risk happens.
terms.example: Switch to air freight for critical items.

terms.example: Hurricane warning within 200 km of the supplier.

terms.meaning: The ability to keep going and recover quickly after a disruption.
terms.example: Rerouting through another port within days.

terms.meaning: The ability to change direction quickly.
Knowing where stock, shipments and orders are in real time.
terms.example: Tracking every container on a dashboard.

quiz.q: A risk has probability 4 and impact 5. What is its score and level?
quiz.why: 4 × 5 = 20, which is in the Critical band (16–25).

quiz.q: You buy cargo insurance for a valuable shipment. Which strategy is this?
quiz.why: Insurance passes the financial cost of the risk to the insurer.

quiz.q: Two of your suppliers buy their raw material from the same factory. What is the problem?
options: A hidden single point of failure upstream
quiz.why: If that one factory stops, both suppliers stop.

quiz.q: What is a trigger in a contingency plan?
options: A pre-agreed signal that starts an action
quiz.why: Triggers turn decisions under pressure into decisions already made.

quiz.q: The Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal in 2021. Which lesson fits best?
options: Single routes are single points of failure
quiz.why: One blocked route stopped hundreds of ships.

quiz.q: During a crisis, a team wants to order three months of extra stock ‘just in case’. What is the risk?
options: Overstock and expiry later, and a bullwhip effect upstream
quiz.why: Panic buying creates overstock and distorts demand for suppliers.

quiz.q: What does visibility mean in risk management?
options: Knowing where stock, shipments and orders are in real time
quiz.why: You cannot react quickly if you do not know where things are.

quiz.q: How often should operational risks in the register be reviewed?
quiz.why: A register that is not reviewed is only a record of old risks.

quiz.q: A risk scores 2 (probability) × 2 (impact). What is the usual strategy?
quiz.why: Low risks (1–4) are usually accepted and watched.

quiz.q: Only one employee knows how to prepare customs documents. What type of risk is this?
quiz.why: Cross-train others and write the procedure down.

workbook.intro: Use the Risk score and heat map tool in Tools. Think about a company in Qatar.

questions.prompt: List five risks for a Doha company that imports fresh food by sea and air. Give each one a probability and impact score (1–5) and its total score.
questions.hint: Think suppliers, routes, port, cold chain, documents, IT.

questions.prompt: Take your highest risk. Choose a strategy (avoid, reduce, transfer or accept), name an owner and write one trigger.
What did Qatar’s supply chains do well in June 2017? What should importers keep doing today?
questions.hint: Read the Qatar 2017 case in Tools.

questions.prompt: Your warehouse system is hit by ransomware and stops for three days. Write a short plan: what can you still do by hand, who do you tell, and how do you recover?
questions.hint: Paper pick lists, backups, customer messages.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between efficiency and resilience with one example. When is it worth paying for resilience?
